section_summary: This section combines wartime economic intelligence on Japanese banking and the state-directed expansion of shipbuilding, light metals, coal, and iron and steel, including translations of a major Asahi Shimbun series. Later documents report production statistics and strategic industrial locations around Kobe, Yokohama, Tokyo, Korea, and Sakhalin, often from diplomatic or confidential sources. The section also contains interagency correspondence requesting shipyard data and a bibliography on Japanese industrial organization for Civil Affairs planning.

subfiles.title: Continuation: Increased Dividends Declared by the Industrial Bank of Japan
subfiles.from: Japan Times, quoting Toyo Keizai Shimpo
subfiles.about: Explains the wartime growth, investments, financing, profits, and dividend policy of the Industrial Bank of Japan.
subfiles.summary: The continuation traces the bank's rapid loan growth after the outbreak of the China conflict and its increasing holdings of securities and national debt. It explains that industrial debentures guaranteed by the government supplied most of the bank's working funds. Rising profits were used to justify a dividend increase, although management acknowledged pressure to reduce lending rates.

subfiles.title: Memorandum Adding Material to Istanbul Despatch No. 7
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.to: Department of State file
subfiles.about: Directs that information supplied by former Argentine Embassy attaché Ramón Lavalle be added to the Istanbul despatch on Japanese wartime industry.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum refers to Istanbul despatch no. 7 of March 9, 1943. It states that Ramón Lavalle, formerly a special attaché at the Argentine Embassy in Tokyo, requested that the attached items be added to that report.

subfiles.title: Evaluation of Assets of Persons Changing or Discontinuing Their Occupation
subfiles.from: Japanese Ministry of Commerce and Industry and Nichi Nichi newspaper
subfiles.to: Supplement to Istanbul despatch no. 7
subfiles.about: Describes official Japanese standards for valuing the property of retailers compelled to change or discontinue their occupations.
subfiles.summary: The Ministry of Commerce and Industry instructed prefectural authorities to adopt standardized valuations prepared by an expert committee. The rules covered merchandise, real estate, machinery, fixtures, vehicles, and other business assets, with the People's Welfare Bank accepting assessments made under the scheme. A table supplies basic compensation amounts for numerous classes of small retailers.

subfiles.title: Increased Dividends Declared by the Industrial Bank of Japan
subfiles.from: Japan Times, quoting Toyo Keizai Shimpo
subfiles.to: Supplement to Istanbul despatch no. 7
subfiles.about: Reviews the financial expansion that allowed the Industrial Bank of Japan to raise its dividend from six to seven percent.
subfiles.summary: The article attributes the bank's success to Toyotarō Yūki's depression-era industrial lending and to the enormous expansion of wartime credit after 1937. Loans, discounted bills, securities holdings, and profits all rose sharply, while government-guaranteed industrial debentures provided the main working funds. The increased dividend was financially modest but could create pressure for lower loan-interest rates.

subfiles.title: Translations of Important Sections of Zenkoku Kojo Tsuran
subfiles.from: N. W. Pettigrew, Chief, Far Eastern Unit, Military Intelligence Service
subfiles.to: Listed military, diplomatic, economic-warfare, and civilian agencies
subfiles.about: Reports progress in translating the 1939 Japanese national factory directory and proposes wider interagency support for the project.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes Zenkoku Kojo Tsuran as an official directory of factories employing five or more people, organized by industry and location. The Far Eastern Unit had translated or was translating 327 pages covering machinery, explosives, government enterprises, metals, and engines, although the 1939 edition omitted aircraft manufacturers. Pettigrew proposes distributing the translations widely and suggests that another agency take over the low-priority project because of personnel shortages.

subfiles.title: Routing Memorandum for September 7 Report on Japanese Industries
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.to: Department of State staff
subfiles.about: Orders the underlying September 7 report on Japanese industries attached and entered under the appropriate Johansen reference number.
subfiles.summary: This brief internal memorandum concerns the filing and handling of a report on Japanese industries dated September 7, 1943. Its handwritten text directs staff to annex the report and notify or assign the appropriate Johansen number.

subfiles.title: Letter Enclosing Translations on Four Japanese Primary Industries
subfiles.from: John M. Allison, Economic Warfare Division, London
subfiles.to: N. H. Gates, Chief, Economic Intelligence Division, Office of Economic Warfare
subfiles.about: Transmits translations of Asahi Shimbun articles on Japanese iron and steel, coal, light metals, and shipbuilding.
subfiles.summary: Allison encloses articles on four of Japan's five designated primary industries, noting that the aircraft article had already been sent. The translations came from the British Ministry of Economic Warfare, which had obtained them from the Ministry of Information in New Delhi.

subfiles.title: The Five Great Primary Industries: Shipbuilding
subfiles.from: Asahi Shimbun, translated by H. C. Hainworth
subfiles.to: British and United States economic-intelligence recipients
subfiles.about: Describes the interdependence, centralized control, standardization, and financing of Japan's wartime shipbuilding industry.
subfiles.summary: The article stresses shipbuilding's dependence on steel and nearly every other modern industry and identifies Mitsubishi Heavy Industries as Japan's leading builder. The Shipbuilding Control Company coordinated materials and related industries under Kōshirō Shiba and a reserve vice admiral. Naval and merchant construction were placed under unified wartime direction, while standardized ship designs, one-type-per-yard production, centralized ordering, and government financial guarantees were intended to accelerate output.

subfiles.title: The Five Great Primary Industries: Light Metals
subfiles.from: Asahi Shimbun, translated by H. C. Hainworth
subfiles.to: British and United States economic-intelligence recipients
subfiles.about: Surveys Japanese aluminum and magnesium production, raw materials, industrial controls, technology, and expansion plans.
subfiles.summary: The article links aluminum and magnesium production directly to the aircraft program and describes Japan's dependence on bauxite from Southeast Asia as well as lower-grade resources in Manchuria, North China, and Korea. The Light Metals Control Company and Ministry of Commerce supervised production, equipment use, and technical exchanges, including wider adoption of a Yokohama refining process. It also describes projected aluminum expansion in Korea and Formosa and plans to reorganize magnesium production around extraction from seawater.

subfiles.title: The Five Great Primary Industries: Coal
subfiles.from: Asahi Shimbun, translated by H. C. Hainworth
subfiles.to: British and United States economic-intelligence recipients
subfiles.about: Reviews coal resources, companies, pricing, labor, distribution, and plans to reorganize Japanese wartime coal production.
subfiles.summary: The article catalogs coalfields and mines in Japan, Manchuria, North China, and French Indochina and explains the strategic emphasis on supplies less dependent on maritime transport. The Coal Control Company and Nippon Coal Company administered production quotas, pooled prices, distribution, materials, food, and labor, including Korean workers and the Patriotic Labour Corps. Government subsidies offset rising costs, while priority allocation and consolidation of hundreds of small collieries were presented as essential to increasing war potential.

subfiles.title: The Five Great Primary Industries: Iron and Steel
subfiles.from: Asahi Shimbun, translated by H. C. Hainworth
subfiles.to: British and United States economic-intelligence recipients
subfiles.about: Describes Japan's drive for wartime iron-and-steel self-sufficiency through centralized control, expanded continental production, scrap collection, and factory supervision.
subfiles.summary: The article presents the 1940 U.S. export prohibition as the stimulus for eliminating Japanese dependence on imported ore, pig iron, steel, and scrap. It details the Iron and Steel Control Company's membership and its production, raw-material, and marketing organizations in Japan and Manchuria. Proposed remedies for shortages included greater ore and scrap collection, expanded imports from Manchuria, small furnaces near mines, and closer government control of plants. The final pages describe leadership changes and Teijirō Toyoda's effort to emphasize execution of production plans.

subfiles.title: Telegram Reporting Japanese Steel, Aluminum, and Fuel Output
subfiles.from: Harrison, Bern
subfiles.to: Supply and Blockade Division, Washington
subfiles.about: Relays German Armaments Ministry claims about increases in Japanese steel, aluminum, and motor-fuel production.
subfiles.summary: The telegram cites German official Walter Schieber as claiming that Japanese annual steel output had risen from three million prewar tons to eight million tons. It also reports large aluminum production and motor-fuel output of two million tons annually, though the aluminum figure is partly garbled in the OCR. The message was repeated to London.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Japanese Transport and Industrial Production
subfiles.from: U.S. mission, Bern
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, Washington
subfiles.about: Summarizes German press reports on Japanese transport performance and production of aircraft, ships, light metals, and special steel.
subfiles.summary: The telegram reports that Japan fulfilled 96 percent of its first-quarter transport plan, while exceeding the previous year's performance. Asahi Shimbun attributed increased aircraft, ship, and light-metal output partly to heavy rainfall and added hydroelectric power, with new power plants expected to permit more aluminum capacity. Special-steel production was also said to be substantially above the previous year; the surviving text ends during a reference to an agreement involving Korea.

subfiles.title: FBI Letter Transmitting Toyo-Nikki Information on Japanese Industry
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Transmits a memorandum derived from the 1939 Japanese yearbook Toyo-Nikki.
subfiles.summary: Hoover states that the enclosed memorandum was prepared in response to a Foreign Economic Administration request. Copies were also supplied to that agency and the Department of Commerce, with additional copies directed to naval and military intelligence. The referenced memorandum does not appear on this page.

subfiles.title: FBI Letter Transmitting Information on Kobe
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards a confidential-source report and aerial views concerning piers, warehouses, railways, public buildings, and the Kawasaki shipyards at Kobe.
subfiles.summary: The letter says the source lived in Japan in an official capacity until mid-1942 and supplied strategic information about Kobe. Two aerial views reportedly identified the pier district, Kawasaki shipyards, the Prefeitura, and the elevated railway connecting Tokyo and Shimonoseki. The information was also sent to the Foreign Economic Administration and military and naval intelligence.

subfiles.title: Report on Japanese Industry and Strategic Facilities at Kobe
subfiles.from: Confidential source interviewed at Salvador, Bahia
subfiles.to: Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Describes Kobe's port, warehouses, Kawasaki shipyards, railway, and relationship to the Osaka industrial area.
subfiles.summary: The source characterized Kobe as Japan's most important port and the maritime outlet for Osaka, then the country's leading industrial center. He located large piers, concrete warehouses used for troops, the Kawasaki shipyards, the Prefeitura, and the railway through Kobe to Osaka and the Tokyo–Shimonoseki route. Osaka, Tokyo, and Nagoya were ranked as Japan's most important industrial centers.

subfiles.title: Request for Yard-by-Yard Japanese Shipbuilding Data
subfiles.from: Robert P. Terrill, Acting Assistant Chief, Commodities Division
subfiles.to: Captain L. B. Pearse, Bureau of Operations, Navy Department
subfiles.about: Requests merchant- and naval-construction data for each major Japanese shipyard to support a Civil Affairs study.
subfiles.summary: The Commodities Division was studying concentration of ownership in major Japanese industries for Civil Affairs planning. Terrill asks the Navy for yard-by-yard merchant and naval construction data so the division can assess the importance of corporate combines in shipbuilding.

subfiles.title: FBI Letter Transmitting Memorandum on Yokohama Industries
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Transmits a September 25 memorandum containing limited information on industrial locations in Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: Hoover forwards a memorandum prepared at Rio de Janeiro from a reliable confidential source. The same information was being supplied to the American Embassy in Brazil, the Foreign Economic Administration, and military and naval intelligence.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Industrial Locations in Yokohama
subfiles.from: Confidential Source A, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.to: Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Reports commonly known port, railway, munitions, and industrial locations in and near Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: The source described Yokohama as Japan's second most important seaport and noted its four-track electric railway connection with Tokyo. He located a munitions plant between the cities that was reportedly hit during the Doolittle raid. Yokohama itself had textile, glass, silk, and chemical manufacturing, while extensive unidentified industrial activity and colored fires were visible northeast across the harbor.

subfiles.title: Letter Requesting a Bibliography on Japanese Industrial Organization
subfiles.from: Robert P. Terrill, Acting Assistant Chief, Commodities Division
subfiles.to: Robert P. Gooch, Chief, General Reference and Bibliography Division, Library of Congress
subfiles.about: Requests preparation of a bibliography of German sources on Japanese industrial organization for a Civil Affairs guide.
subfiles.summary: Terrill confirms discussions involving Walter M. Rudolph, Eleanor M. Hadley, Gooch, and Taube concerning the proposed bibliography. The work would support a Civil Affairs Guide on the Japanese cartel system. Rudolph was made available to discuss scope and format, and the Department requested access at the earliest convenient date.

subfiles.title: Santiago Despatch Transmitting Legal Attaché Report on Conditions in Japan
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, United States Embassy, Santiago
subfiles.to: Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Transmits a Legal Attaché report based on interviews with former residents and diplomats from Japan.
subfiles.summary: The despatch encloses a December 4, 1944 report concerning information supplied by former Chilean minister Armando Labra Carvajal and White Russian brothers Eugenio and Miguel Sisikin. It recommends sharing the substance with the Foreign Economic Administration. Copies were also provided to the embassy's military, naval, and legal attachés.

subfiles.title: Legal Attaché Report on Japanese Industry
subfiles.from: Legal Attaché, Santiago
subfiles.to: United States Embassy and Department of State
subfiles.about: Compiles interviews with former diplomats and residents concerning dispersed production, shortages, and industrial facilities in Japan, Korea, and Sakhalin.
subfiles.summary: Carlos Porras Cáceres could provide little recent information, but the report identifies several Chilean diplomats and consular officers who had returned from East Asia. Armando Labra described household-based piecework, widely dispersed production, severe food shortages, black-market dependence, and scarce provisions aboard a Japanese exchange ship. Eugenio and Miguel Sisikin identified reported aircraft, automobile, shipbuilding, underground-hangar, factory, and synthetic-oil sites around Yokohama, Tsurumi, Chongjin, Toyohara, and Sakhalin. The surviving pages are discontinuous, moving from the opening of the report to an internally numbered later page.
